verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.28 by Gita Press numbering, where the verse holds both 'kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo...' and 'dṛṣṭvemaṃ svajanaṃ...' (Govindacharya's Ramanuja numbers it the same). Shankara's text (Mahadeva Sastri) and Sridhara's (Vireswarananda) attach the 'kṛpayā' half to 1.27, so their 1.28 is 'seeing these kinsmen... my limbs fail, my mouth is parched'.
attribution_note: Mixed speakers. The first half (kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdann idam abravīt) is Sanjaya narrating to Dhritarashtra; only the second half, after 'arjuna uvāca', is Arjuna speaking to Krishna. Govindacharya's translation of Ramanuja's text makes this explicit (Arjuna, overcome by compassion, became sad and spoke). Our Sanskrit places 'arjuna uvāca' at the very start, but it belongs between the two halves. Suggest speaker 'Sanjaya, then Arjuna'.
translation_note: Our translation turns Sanjaya's description ('filled with deep pity, despairing, he said this') into Arjuna's first-person 'I am overcome with pity and sorrow'. Arjuna's own sentence only begins in this verse ('Krishna, seeing these my own people standing here, eager to fight...') and is completed in 1.29 (my limbs give way, my mouth dries). Suggested: 'Overcome by deep pity, sinking in despair, Arjuna said: Krishna, when I see my own people standing here eager to fight...'.
context: Arjuna has asked Krishna to drive the chariot between the two armies so he can see whom he must fight; Krishna stops before Bhishma and Drona and tells him to look. Arjuna sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, friends and in-laws on both sides. Here Sanjaya reports that pity overwhelms him and he begins to speak; in the following verses his body gives way, his bow slips, he argues against the war and finally sits down in the chariot, refusing to fight.

key_terms.sense: pervaded by an extreme pity or compassion
sinking in despondency, dejected
one's own people, kin
assembled here and eager to fight

core_teaching: Not yet a teaching but the crisis that prompts the Gita: love and pity for people on the other side overwhelm even the greatest warrior. Commentators read the pity differently, Ramanuja as noble compassion and fear of wrongdoing, the Advaita line as grief born of seeing bodies as 'mine'.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898 (summary closing ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: Calls Arjuna most noble and compassionate: though the Kauravas had plotted to kill the Pandavas (the lac house), he saw them as kin, was overcome by pity and fear of wrongdoing, and sat down refusing to fight.
Introduces Arjuna's speech, which runs to the end of the chapter: seeing his kinsmen drawn up to fight, his limbs, hands and feet give way and his mouth goes completely dry.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, introduction at 2.10, not a comment on this verse
commentaries.gist: Gives no comment on chapter 1. His introduction at 2.10 reads the whole passage up to 2.9 as grief and delusion born of 'I am theirs and they are mine', which cause samsara and are removed only by self-knowledge.

practical_reading: Teachers use this moment to normalise breakdown: the Gita opens with its hero shaking, not with a lecture. Freezing when a conflict involves people you love is human, and the first step is to say honestly what is happening, as Arjuna does to Krishna.
misreadings: Not a portrait of cowardice: Ramanuja stresses Arjuna's compassion and righteousness here.
Not Arjuna's own claim of pity; that half is Sanjaya's narration.
Not a teaching about whether to fight one's family; it is a narrative moment that the rest of the Gita answers.
cautions: Setting is a war against one's own family; may stir pain for readers in family conflict or estrangement.
The Advaita reading calls this pity delusion; avoid telling a distressed reader that their compassion is a fault.
speaks_to: Freezing when a conflict involves family or people you love
Physical overwhelm before a hard confrontation (shaking, dry mouth, weak limbs)
Feeling ashamed of breaking down when others expect you to be strong
Disputes with relatives, old mentors or close colleagues
not_for: Someone in an abusive family situation who might read it as a nudge to confront or 'fight' family
A reader looking for a clear answer or instruction; the verse offers none yet
research_note: Shankara has no commentary on chapter 1; his 2.10 introduction is used instead. The earlier draft also cited Madhusudana Sarasvati; that came from a source we no longer use and was dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.2 (same numbering in Shankara/Mahadeva Sastri, Ramanuja/Govindacharya, Sridhara/Vireswarananda and Sivananda).
translation_note: Fair. 'Faintness of heart' for kaśmalam is acceptable; Sridhara glosses it as a confusion that has overtaken him, Sivananda translates 'dejection', Govindacharya's Ramanuja 'ill-timed melancholy'. Sridhara explains asvargyam as unrighteous (not leading to heaven).
context: Sanjaya has just described Arjuna in tears, overcome by pity (2.1). These are Krishna's first words in the Gita: a sharp question about where this collapse came from. The rebuke continues in 2.3; Arjuna then lays out his dilemma (2.4-2.8) and at 2.7 asks to be taught.

key_terms.sense: a clouding of mind, dejection (Sridhara: a confusion that has overtaken him)
in a crisis, at a perilous moment
not practised by noble people
does not lead to heaven; brings disgrace

core_teaching: Krishna questions the timing and source of Arjuna's collapse: at the decisive moment he has slid into a confusion that noble people do not indulge and that serves neither this life nor the next.

commentaries.gist: Asks from what cause this confusion has come over Arjuna in a crisis; it is not something honourable people take up, it does not lead to heaven, meaning it is unrighteous, and it brings disrepute.

Reads 2.2-2.3 together: Krishna rebukes a sadness felt out of place, not approved by the wise, harmful to higher aims, inglorious and born of a faint heart, and urges him to shake it off and stand up to fight.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, introduction at 2.10
commentaries.gist: Does not comment on 2.2; his introduction at 2.10 treats everything up to 2.9 as the display of grief and delusion that the teaching from 2.11 removes.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as a wake-up question rather than contempt: when you notice yourself shutting down exactly when action matters, ask where the paralysis came from instead of simply obeying it.
misreadings: Not a model for shaming someone's tears or fear.
Not Krishna's whole answer: he starts by appealing to honour and duty, and the deeper teaching begins at 2.11 (Shankara's 2.10 introduction).
cautions: The tone is a rebuke; for a reader in grief, depression or burnout it can feel like being scolded for struggling.
Words like 'disgrace' and 'ignoble' can feed shame.
speaks_to: Freezing or backing out at a decisive moment (an exam, interview, hard conversation) and wanting a firm nudge
Someone who has asked a friend to be blunt with them
Noticing that a sudden doubt is really fear
not_for: Fresh grief or bereavement
Depression or burnout, where a reprimand lands as blame
Someone already flooded with shame
research_note: Earlier draft cited Abhinavagupta and Madhusudana from a source we no longer use; dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (same numbering in all four archive.org editions checked).
translation_note: 'Unmanliness' for klaibyam is the standard literal rendering (Mahadeva Sastri also uses it; Sivananda has 'impotence'). Sridhara glosses it as cowardice, and Govindacharya's Ramanuja renders it 'get thou not unnerved'. For a modern, mixed audience 'loss of nerve' or 'faint-heartedness' is faithful and avoids a gendered reading.
context: Krishna continues the opening rebuke of 2.2. He addresses Arjuna as Partha, son of Pritha, and as 'scorcher of foes', recalling who he is. Arjuna replies in 2.4 by asking how he could shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he should revere.

key_terms.sense: impotence, loss of nerve (Sridhara: cowardice; Govindacharya's Ramanuja: being unnerved)
petty weakness of heart
stand up, rise
scorcher of foes: a reminder of his strength

core_teaching: This faint-heartedness is not who Arjuna is; it is small and can be thrown off. Krishna calls him to stand up, before giving any reasons, which come later.

commentaries.gist: Glosses klaibyam as cowardice: do not be overcome by it, it does not befit you; shake off this mean, contemptible faint-heartedness and rise for battle, chastiser of foes.

Treats 2.2-2.3 together: a sadness out of season, unworthy and springing from weakness of heart; Krishna tells him to shake it off and stand up. Arjuna, still gripped by affection, pity and fear of wrongdoing, does not accept this.
Translates klaibyam as 'impotence' and the rest as a call to cast off mean weakness of heart and stand up; offers no separate comment on this verse.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as the line a true friend says once: this smallness is not you. Name the shrinking, stand up, and take the next step; the reasons can follow.
misreadings: Not 'feelings are weakness' or 'man up'.
Not a statement about gender; Sridhara glosses klaibya as cowardice, i.e. loss of nerve.
Not the whole answer: the reasoned teaching begins at 2.11.
cautions: 'Unmanliness' can read as gendered shaming; consider 'faint-heartedness'.
A rebuke; not for acute grief or a reader who is already blaming themselves.
speaks_to: Talking yourself out of something you are capable of
Cold feet before a commitment or a performance
Needing a push after a long period of hesitation
not_for: Clinical depression, trauma or panic responses
Grief
Someone being pressured into a fight they would be wise to walk away from
research_note: Shankara does not comment on 2.3. Earlier draft cited Madhusudana from a source we no longer use; dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.6 (same numbering in all editions checked).
attribution_note: Speaker (Arjuna) and listener (Krishna) are right, but our `setting` reads 'Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed...', which describes Krishna's verses. Suggest: 'Arjuna, slumped in the chariot, tells Krishna he cannot see which choice is right.'
translation_note: Acceptable. Mahadeva Sastri's translation of Shankara's text adds a gloss that the two options are living on alms without killing versus fighting; Govindacharya's Ramanuja likewise reads 'begged food or blood-bought food?'. Sridhara reads the alternatives as winning or losing. Either way the verse is Arjuna's confusion, not a teaching.
context: Arjuna has refused to fight, asking how he could attack Bhishma and Drona and saying it would be better to live on alms than enjoy blood-stained wealth (2.4-2.5). Here he admits he cannot even tell which course is better. In 2.7 he confesses his confusion and asks Krishna to teach him as a disciple.

key_terms.sense: which of the two is weightier, better for us
whether we win, or they win
we would not wish to go on living

core_teaching: Arjuna voices a double uncertainty: he cannot judge which path is right or what the outcome will be, and even victory would be hollow because it would cost the lives of the people he loves.

commentaries.gist: Even if they chose the unrighteous course, they could not say whether victory or defeat would be better; in fact victory would be defeat, since the very people without whom they would not wish to live stand before them.

Summarising 2.4-2.8: Arjuna thinks it more honourable to be killed by the Kauravas than to win unjustly; he humbly asks Krishna, as disciple and refuge-seeker, what is truly best, and Krishna sees his pity is misplaced.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, text and translator's gloss
commentaries.gist: No commentary on this verse; the translator's gloss frames the choice as begging without killing versus fighting as duty. Shankara's 2.10 introduction treats this whole section as grief and delusion.

practical_reading: Teachers point out that honest not-knowing is where real guidance starts: Arjuna's admission that he cannot see the right choice leads straight to his asking for help in the next verse.
misreadings: Not the Gita's conclusion that victory is worthless; it is Arjuna's confusion, which Krishna goes on to answer.
Should not be quoted as Krishna's teaching.
cautions: Contains 'we would not wish to live' after killing loved ones; avoid foregrounding this phrase for a reader who may be having thoughts of not wanting to live.
speaks_to: Being stuck between two bad options
Decisions where 'winning' would hurt people you love (family business, inheritance, divorce, a dispute with relatives)
Not knowing what success would even look like
The moment just before asking for help
not_for: Someone expressing they do not want to live
Someone who needs reassurance that their choice is right
research_note: Earlier draft cited Madhusudana and Abhinavagupta from a source we no longer use; dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.8 (same numbering in all editions checked).
attribution_note: Speaker (Arjuna) and listener (Krishna) are right, but our `setting` reads 'Krishna to Arjuna...'. Suggest: 'Arjuna tells Krishna that nothing he could win would heal this grief.'
translation_note: Good. Our_note attributes the reading to 'Shankara's introduction'; Shankara does not comment on 2.8 itself, but his introduction at 2.10 says grief and delusion are ended only by self-knowledge, so the note is fair if worded that way.
context: Having asked to be taught as Krishna's disciple (2.7), Arjuna explains why he needs help: nothing he can imagine gaining would remove this grief. In 2.9 he declares he will not fight and falls silent; Krishna, smiling as it were, begins the teaching at 2.11.

key_terms.sense: grief that dries up, withers the senses
could drive away, remove
an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom
lordship over the gods

core_teaching: Arjuna recognises that his grief is not the kind any outward gain can fix, not even the greatest kingdom on earth or in heaven. Commentators see this honest admission as the starting point of the inner teaching.

commentaries.gist: Told to decide for himself, Arjuna replies he sees no action that would remove a grief drying up his senses, even with everything coveted: an unrivalled kingdom on earth or lordship over the gods.

Krishna sees Arjuna made helpless by misplaced affection and pity, mistaking a lawful war for wrong; he resolves that only knowledge of the self, joined with action done without interest in results, will lift this confusion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, introduction at 2.10, not a comment on this verse
commentaries.gist: Reads 1.2 to 2.9 as showing grief and delusion, the cause of samsara; since nothing but self-knowledge ends them, Krishna begins his teaching at 2.11.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to name grief that no achievement, purchase or distraction can touch, and to say that admitting this is the first step toward a different kind of help.
misreadings: Not a statement that grief is hopeless: in the Gita this admission opens the teaching.
Not a rejection of worldly success as such.
cautions: Vivid grief imagery; good for naming grief, but best paired with what follows (2.11 onward) so it does not end in despair.
speaks_to: Grief or heartbreak that success does not touch
Burnout where achievements feel empty
Realising you need a different kind of help, not more of the same
not_for: Someone looking for quick motivation
A reader at risk of hopelessness, if used alone without the verses that answer it
research_note: Earlier draft cited Madhusudana (with a Chandogya Upanishad parallel) from a source we no longer use; dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.11 (same numbering in Shankara/Mahadeva Sastri, Ramanuja/Govindacharya, Sridhara/Vireswarananda and Sivananda).
translation_note: Good. Our_note says 'Shankara: this verse is the seed of the whole teaching'; Shankara's introduction at 2.10 actually calls grief and delusion the cause of samsara and says Krishna begins at 2.11 to remove them (Sivananda says the Gita's philosophy begins here). Our_note's 'gentle irony' is not in the commentaries checked; the smile is in 2.10. Shankara does say Arjuna shows folly and wisdom side by side.
context: Arjuna has said 'I will not fight' and fallen silent (2.9); Krishna, as if smiling (2.10), now begins the teaching proper. This verse opens the section on the deathless self that runs to 2.30, followed by arguments from duty (2.31-38).

key_terms.sense: you have grieved for those who are not to be grieved for
words that sound wise, talk of the learned (Sridhara: words befitting the wise)
those whose life-breath has gone and those whose has not: the dead and the living
the wise; Shankara: those whose understanding is of the self

core_teaching: Krishna points to the contradiction between Arjuna's grief and his learned arguments: those who know what the self truly is do not grieve as he does, for the dead or the living. It sets up the teaching that the self is eternal and the body changes by nature.

commentaries.gist: Bhishma and Drona need no grief: they are good men and eternal in their real nature. Arjuna mourns yet talks like the wise, showing folly and wisdom together; knowers of the self mourn neither living nor dead.

Arjuna's talk of ancestors losing offerings (1.42) assumes a soul distinct from the body, yet he grieves. For those who know the true natures of body and soul, neither the lifeless body nor the living soul is cause for grief.

Arjuna's grief comes from not discriminating self from body. He mourns kin who are not truly objects of sorrow and, though rebuked at 2.2, keeps uttering learned-sounding words without being wise; the wise grieve for neither dead nor living.

Says the Gita's philosophy begins here. Bhishma and Drona are eternal in their real nature; knowers of the self do not mourn living or dead because they know the self is unborn and death is only the body's disintegration.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as an invitation to look at what grief is attached to: the changing body and circumstances, or the person's deeper being, which the Gita says does not end. Many stress it answers grief that has frozen Arjuna in the middle of his duty, not the ordinary tears of loss.
misreadings: Not 'don't cry' or 'your grief is wrong'.
Not contempt for mourners; the point concerns knowing the self, not suppressing feeling.
Not 'the dead don't matter'.
cautions: Literally tells the listener not to grieve; on Day 1 of a grief plan it would land as dismissive.
The eternal-self frame can feel like a brush-off to fresh loss.
The line ('talking like you know better') can feel scolding.
speaks_to: Grief that has become paralysis and stops someone doing what must be done
Anticipatory grief, fear of losing someone
Readers ready to ask what in a person does not die
Overthinking that dresses fear in clever arguments
not_for: Fresh bereavement (first days or weeks)
Loss of a child, or loss to suicide
Anyone already being told by others to 'move on'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.12 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. Our_note's Shankara and Ramanuja summaries match the commentaries.
context: Krishna's first argument after 2.11 for why the wise do not grieve. It is followed by the image of the self passing through childhood, youth and old age into another body (2.13) and the advice to endure passing heat and cold (2.14).

key_terms.sense: never was there a time I did not exist
rulers of men, the kings on the field
(nor) shall we cease to be hereafter

core_teaching: None of them, Krishna, Arjuna or the kings, ever began to exist or will cease to exist: the self persists through past, present and future, so death of the body is not the end of the person.

commentaries.gist: I, you and these kings existed through past births and deaths and will continue after these bodies die: as the self we are eternal in all three times. The plural refers to different bodies, not many selves.

As the Lord has always existed, so have Arjuna and all these souls, and all will exist forever. Spoken by a teacher removing ignorance, the 'I, you, all of us' shows that souls are many and distinct from God.

The Lord, though his body of divine play appears and disappears, is beginningless; Arjuna and the kings, being parts of him, always existed and always will. Having no birth or death, they need no grief.
Speaks of the immortality of the soul: it exists in past, present and future, and a person continues to exist after the physical body dies; there is life beyond.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as perspective on identity: the 'you' that persists through childhood, youth and age is more than passing circumstances, so loss and change do not erase who someone is.
misreadings: Not a claim that bodies or personalities are permanent.
Not a reason to treat life or death lightly because 'no one really dies'.
cautions: About death and continuity of the self; comforting to some, abstract or dismissive to others in fresh grief.
Schools differ (one self appearing as many, or many real selves); avoid presenting one view as the only meaning.
speaks_to: Fear of death
Wondering whether a loved one who has died still exists
Existential anxiety, a sense of being more than one's roles
not_for: A reader of another faith or none, in acute grief, who may experience it as doctrine imposed
Someone who needs practical, not metaphysical, help right now

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.15 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. 'These' (ete) refers to the sense-contacts of 2.14 that bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain; worth making explicit in a reading.
context: Krishna has said the self passes through childhood, youth and age (2.13) and that the contacts of the senses bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go and must be endured (2.14). This verse gives the reason to endure them; 2.16 then distinguishes the unreal from the real.

key_terms.sense: do not distress, do not shake
the same in pain and pleasure
steady, wise, composed
becomes fit for immortality, i.e. liberation

core_teaching: The person who is not knocked over by the passing contacts of pleasure and pain, and holds steady through both, becomes fit for freedom. Endurance grounded in understanding, not mere toughness, is the point.

commentaries.gist: The wise person who neither exults in pleasure nor sinks in pain, unaffected by heat and cold because he sees the eternal self, and who bears the opposites calmly, becomes fit for immortality, meaning liberation.

A courageous person who regards unavoidable pain as equal to pleasure is untroubled by blows; for such a one, doing the duties of his station without seeking reward leads to immortality, not for one who cannot bear pain.

Rather than trying to remedy the sense-contacts, one should simply endure them, since that yields a great result; the person not overpowered by them, unperturbed in pleasure and pain, becomes fit for liberation through knowledge.

Pleasure and pain come from identifying the self with the body. Endurance (titiksha) builds will-power and is a qualification on the path of knowledge; alone it does not liberate, but joined with discrimination and dispassion it leads to immortality.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as training in equanimity: let good and bad days come and go without letting either decide who you are, and build the steadiness to keep doing what matters through both.
misreadings: Not numbness or hiding what you feel.
Not a demand to tolerate harm that can and should be stopped; the examples are unavoidable passing experiences (heat, cold, pleasure, pain).
cautions: A reader in acute pain may hear 'stay the same in pain' as being told their suffering is a failure of composure.
speaks_to: Mood swings tied to success and failure
Long stretches of discomfort that must be borne (recovery, caregiving, exam preparation)
Wanting to be less reactive
not_for: Someone enduring abuse who needs permission to leave, not to endure
Acute grief or crisis, where 'be the same in pain and pleasure' sounds dismissive

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.16 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. 'Final word' for antaḥ matches Ramanuja's gloss (anta = the conclusive end, i.e. the essential nature, of each). Our_note follows Shankara and Sridhara (heat, cold and their causes as the unreal). Ramanuja reads asat/sat differently, as the changing body versus the constant soul.
context: After telling Arjuna to endure passing pleasure and pain (2.14-15), Krishna gives the principle behind it: what is unreal has no being and what is real never stops being. The next verses (2.17-18) say that what pervades all is imperishable while bodies come to an end, so 'fight'.

key_terms.sense: the unreal has no being
the real has no non-being
the final truth, the settled conclusion
by those who see things as they are

core_teaching: What changes and passes, such as heat, cold, pleasure, pain and the body, does not have real being; what is truly real, the self, never ceases. Seeing this difference makes endurance possible.

commentaries.gist: Heat, cold and their causes are not truly real, being changing effects, as a pot is never perceived apart from clay. What awareness never loses is real, what it loses is unreal; the self is the real.

Asat is the non-sentient body, whose nature is to change; sat is the conscious soul, whose nature is constancy. Seers of truth have settled the essential nature of each, so the body's passing is no ground for grief.

Answers how hard things like heat and cold can be endured: by discrimination. Being non-self, they have no reality in the self; the self, whose nature is being, never ceases; knowers of truth have settled both.

The changeless self alone always exists; the ever-changing world of names and forms is unreal, like a mirage or the snake seen in a rope. The sage sees through name and form to existence-knowledge-bliss.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate what passes (moods, circumstances, praise and blame) from what lasts in you, so that you stop staking your whole self on what is changing.
misreadings: Not 'the world is fake, nothing matters'; even the Advaita reading uses it to ground endurance and right action.
Schools disagree sharply on what the 'unreal' is; avoid presenting one reading as the only one.
cautions: Abstract and philosophical; calling a reader's pain 'unreal' would land badly in distress.
speaks_to: Anxiety about losing status, possessions or approval
Wanting a fixed point when everything is changing
Reflective readers interested in philosophy
not_for: Someone in pain who could hear it as 'your suffering isn't real'
Fresh grief
research_note: Earlier draft included a Madhva reading from a source we no longer use; the downloaded 1906 Madhva bhashya on archive.org is unusable OCR, so Madhva was dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.25 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara and Sridhara.
context: Part of Krishna's description of the self that cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried (2.23-24). This verse closes the description with three more marks and draws the conclusion: do not grieve. From 2.26 he argues that even on the opposite view grief is not fitting.

key_terms.sense: unmanifest, not an object of the senses
unthinkable, beyond the reach of thought
unchangeable
you ought not to grieve

core_teaching: The self is not something the senses grasp, the mind can picture, or anything can alter; knowing it so, there is no ground for grieving over it, or for thinking 'I kill, they are killed'.

commentaries.gist: The self is beyond the senses, so unmanifest; what is not perceived cannot be thought, so unthinkable; having no parts, it cannot change as milk does. Knowing this, do not grieve or see yourself as slayer.

The soul cannot be shown like divisible physical things, nor conceived as having this or that familiar quality; it is a unique kind of entity and so cannot be modified. Knowing this, Arjuna has no cause for grief.

Unmanifest: not an object of the eye and senses; unthinkable: not an object of the mind; unchangeable: not touched by the organs of action. 'Is said to be' brings in scriptural authority for the self's eternity.
Follows Shankara closely: the self cannot be seen, so cannot be thought of, and does not change form like milk turned by buttermilk; so do not mourn, nor think of yourself as slayer.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a reminder that the deepest part of a person is not what illness, ageing or loss can reach, which can steady both the grieving and the dying.
misreadings: Not a prohibition on mourning; it concerns grief over the self being destroyed.
Not a claim that the body or personality is unchanging.
cautions: Ends in 'you should not grieve'; would feel dismissive early in a grief plan.
Assumes an eternal self; can feel like doctrine to a reader who does not share it.
speaks_to: Facing serious illness or ageing in oneself or a loved one
Reflective grief some time after a loss
Fear that a person is 'gone completely'
not_for: The first days of bereavement
A reader who wants practical help, not metaphysics

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.26 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. Our line ('if you believe life simply begins and ends') matches Ramanuja's reading (if you take the self to be just the body); Shankara reads it as the popular view that the self is born and dies again with each body. Both are concessive arguments.
context: Having described the deathless self (2.17-25), Krishna now argues from the other side: suppose Arjuna holds the common view that the self is born and dies. Even so (2.27), birth leads certainly to death and death to birth, so grief over the inevitable is unfitting.

key_terms.sense: and even if: a concession for argument's sake
constantly being born, or constantly dying
you ought not to grieve like this

core_teaching: Even on the view that the self is born and dies with the body, being crushed by grief is not warranted, because birth and death are bound to follow each other.

commentaries.gist: Grants the popular view that the self is born with each body and dies with it; even so Arjuna should not grieve, since death is inevitable for what is born and birth for what has died.
If Arjuna still takes the self to be nothing but the body, constantly born and dying, there is still no ground for grief: for changing bodies, birth and death are an unavoidable law of nature.
Having shown that the self has neither birth nor destruction, Krishna now argues that even if the self were born and died with the body, grief would still be out of place.
Krishna takes up the popular supposition for argument's sake; even then one should not grieve, because birth and death follow each other by an unrelenting law of nature.

Not Krishna's own view of the self; it is a concession for argument.
cautions: Still ends in 'you should not grieve'; time it well after a loss.
Can sound like logic used against feelings.

Grief that has gone on to the point of stopping a person's life
People who find metaphysical comfort unconvincing
not_for: Early grief
A reader whose grief is being policed by others

Fear of death
Reflection on mortality

The first weeks of bereavement

manifest in the middle
whose end is again unmanifest

commentaries.gist: Sons and friends, as bodies, are unseen before birth, seen in the middle, unseen after death. He quotes a consolation verse (came from the unseen and went back; not yours, nor you his) and asks why lament mere appearances.
Beings, though ever-existent, pass from an unmanifest state before birth to a manifest middle and back to the unmanifest; such change is a law of nature and gives no cause for sorrow.

Bodies exist in causal form in the unmanifest (pradhana) before birth, are manifest between birth and death, and dissolve back; grieving them is like someone who has woken up still mourning friends lost in a dream.

Not 'the person was never real'; the dream and illusion comparisons are about the body's passing appearance.

Contemplating one's own mortality
Birth and death in the family prompting big questions
Readers drawn to the mystery of where we come from
not_for: Fresh bereavement

A reader who feels their grief is being minimised

speaks_to: Grief that has settled and is looking for meaning
Loss of an animal companion, read gently (Ramanuja: the same self in all beings)
Fear of death
not_for: Fresh loss
Violent or traumatic death
Readers who might hear it as 'your loss doesn't count'

whose minds are carried off by that (flowery) speech
resolute, one-pointed understanding
does not take root in the mind

'Flowery' speech is pleasant like a flower but bears no further fruit; it is uttered by those devoted to the reward-promising parts of the Veda who deny any goal beyond heaven, and it keeps them in rebirth.

Those who hold heaven as the highest goal speak attractive words about rites that bring enjoyment and power; people carried away by them do not reach the one-pointed resolve that turns the mind wholly toward the Lord.
People clinging to pleasure and power cannot steady the mind or meditate; always planning to acquire wealth and power, they stay restless and lack poised understanding.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to modern distraction: when attention is constantly captured by the promise of more comfort, status or reward, it cannot settle on one clear purpose. Fewer lures make room for focus.

cautions: Can sound moralising to someone already struggling with addiction or compulsive behaviour; frame it as about attention, not character.

Career choices driven only by perks and status
Feeling unable to commit to one path
not_for: Someone in financial hardship, for whom 'chasing comfort' would feel insulting
A reader seeking comfort in grief

free of the pairs of opposites
not preoccupied with acquiring what you lack and guarding what you have
self-possessed, vigilant

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to anxiety about getting and holding on: plan and provide, but do not let acquiring and protecting become the centre of life; keep a clear, steady core beneath the ups and downs.

Feeling pulled between opposites (praise and blame, gain and loss)
Wanting a calmer centre amid ambition

A reader who could take it as advice to neglect responsibilities to family

Performance anxiety tied to outcomes
Students fixated on marks
Feeling empty after achieving targets

A season of disillusionment that is turning into clarity

speaks_to: Paralysis from conflicting advice (career, health, parenting)

the desires that have entered the mind
content in the self, by the self
one whose wisdom is steady

When the mind is wholly occupied with the self and finds satisfaction there, other desires in the heart are banished; this is the highest stage of steady wisdom. The next verses describe lower stages.

A seeker's means of knowledge, once natural, are the marks of the realised. Delighting in the self, whose nature is supreme bliss, one drops desire for paltry things of oneself; that marks steady wisdom.
Someone who has sugar candy does not crave coarse jaggery: one who tastes the bliss of the self does not thirst for sense pleasures, and all the world's pleasures together seem worthless to him.

speaks_to: Restlessness and constant wanting

Seeking contentment that does not depend on circumstances

cautions: 'Without attachment anywhere' (Sridhara: even to sons) can sound cold to parents, caregivers or the newly bereaved.
speaks_to: Emotional swings with good and bad news (results, reviews, markets)
Wanting to respond rather than react
Leaders who need to stay steady for others
not_for: A grieving parent or partner
Someone who already feels emotionally numb or disconnected

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.59 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. the objects fall away
except the relish, the craving for them
on seeing the Highest

Lazy, sick or fasting people also turn from objects, so that alone marks no wisdom. For the body-identified abstainer experience stops but craving stays; in the wise it ends on realising the Supreme.
By austerity and abandoning objects, the objects may turn away from the ascetic, but the longing remains; only knowledge of the self destroys the subtle tendencies (vasanas) and attachments entirely.

Wanting deeper motivation than willpower

Smart people surprised by their own impulses

Irritability over small likes and dislikes

Choosing a quieter, values-led life
Spiritual awakening that changes what matters

Insomnia or literal sleep problems

speaks_to: Older readers wondering if it is too late to change
Facing the end of life with calm
Wanting a lasting, not temporary, peace

Fresh bereavement

tell me decisively that one thing
the highest good

Not Krishna's teaching; it is the student's question.

Wanting one clear next step
Students and seekers who feel they are being told opposite things
not_for: A reader who needs grounding or comfort rather than a question

by mere renunciation alone
perfection, fulfilment

Not 'never rest'.

Procrastination framed as 'waiting until I'm ready'
Spiritual seekers tempted to withdraw from responsibilities
not_for: Someone in burnout who genuinely needs rest or to leave a harmful situation

without doing any action
helplessly, not by one's own choice
by the qualities born of nature (sattva, rajas, tamas)

No one stays still even a moment; resolve to do nothing and the qualities of matter, stirred by past deeds, force action. So karma yoga must first wear away past sin and master the gunas before knowledge is possible.

Renouncing action can only mean being unattached to it, since giving it up is impossible: no one, wise or ignorant, stays inactive even a moment, being driven by attachment and aversion arising from their own nature.
Sattva, rajas and tamas drive the ignorant helplessly to act; sattvic action helps toward liberation while rajasic and tamasic action binds. One who knows the self has crossed beyond the gunas.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to drop the fantasy of a life without demands: you will be doing something every moment anyway, so choose to act well and with the right spirit rather than wishing to escape action.

cautions: 'Helplessly' could feed fatalism in a discouraged reader; pair with 3.7 or 3.34.
speaks_to: Wishing to escape responsibilities
Restlessness and the impossibility of 'doing nothing'
Understanding why habits run themselves
not_for: Someone with depression who feels unable to act and could read 'helplessly' as confirmation

one of deluded mind
one of false conduct, a hypocrite

Showy religiosity
Wanting integrity between thought and action
not_for: Readers with intrusive thoughts or scrupulosity
Someone already harsh on themselves

Building discipline without self-denial theatrics

Team, family or community life where everyone carries part of the load
Environmental care and stewardship

Someone lonely and eating alone

core_teaching: Those who know more should not shake the conviction of people who are growing through their work; instead, by doing the work well themselves, they should encourage others in it.

commentaries.gist: The ignorant believe 'I should do this and enjoy its result'; the wise should not unsettle that conviction, but should do the same work diligently and well himself and so get them to do theirs.

The unwise are seekers who cannot yet take up the path of knowledge, for whom works are the sole means. The wise should not unsettle them but enter wholeheartedly into works to encourage them by example.

Objection: shouldn't the wise, out of pity, teach them the self is a non-agent? No: that would turn them from work before knowledge arises, leaving them with neither. Make them work, by working carefully yourself.

Do not unsettle the belief of those who work for fruit; set an example by doing your duties diligently without attachment, encourage them in their duties, and once their hearts are purified, sow the seeds of selfless service.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to mentoring, parenting and teaching: meet people at their stage, don't knock down a beginner's motivation with advanced ideas, and lead by example rather than lecture.
misreadings: Not a licence to withhold honest information or keep people in the dark for one's own benefit.
Not elitism; the motive given is kindness to the learner.
cautions: 'The ignorant' can sound condescending; soften in readings.
speaks_to: Teachers, managers, parents, senior colleagues
Someone eager to share a new insight that might discourage others
Leading by example
not_for: Situations of abuse or deception, where 'don't unsettle them' could be misused to justify silence

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.27 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara.
context: Explains the inner difference between the wise and the unwise, who may do the same work (3.25-26). Next, 3.28 says the knower of the gunas and their functions sees that 'gunas act upon gunas' and is not attached.

key_terms.sense: by the qualities of nature (expressed as body, senses, mind)
actions being done
one whose mind is deluded by ego
'I am the doer'

core_teaching: All activity is carried out by nature's forces working through body, senses and mind; it is the ego's confusion that claims, 'I alone am doing this.'

commentaries.gist: All actions are done by the gunas, nature's modifications appearing as body and senses. One whose mind is deluded by ego identifies with body and senses, takes on their attributes, and through ignorance thinks 'I am the doer'.
Activities arise from matter's three qualities; one blinded by ahamkara, the mistaken notion that the non-self body is the self, takes the body's doings for the self's and thinks 'I am the doer'.

Answers 'if the wise must act too, how do they differ from the ignorant?': actions are done by the senses, products of nature, but the ignorant, superimposing the self on the senses through ego, thinks 'I am doing this'.

Nature is the balance of sattva, rajas and tamas; when it is disturbed, body, senses and mind form. Deluded by ego, a person identifies with these, ascribes their attributes to the self, and thinks 'I am the doer'.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to pride and anxiety alike: much of what we do rides on forces and help beyond us, so hold both credit and blame more lightly and act without the burden of being the sole doer.
misreadings: Not a denial of moral responsibility ('nature did it, not me').
Not 'nothing I do matters'.
cautions: Could be misused to excuse harmful behaviour; frame it as freedom from ego, not from accountability.
speaks_to: Perfectionism and over-responsibility
Pride in success, or crushing self-blame for failure
Wanting to work with less ego
not_for: Someone trying to avoid accountability for harm done
A reader who already feels powerless

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.33 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara, including the objection he raises and answers with 3.34. Nature (prakṛti) here means one's ingrained disposition from past impressions, not 'nature' in the outdoor sense.
context: Krishna has urged Arjuna to act, surrendering all action to him (3.30-32), and warned that those who reject this teaching are lost. This verse explains why many do not follow it: beings follow their nature. 3.34 immediately says not to fall under the sway of like and dislike, and 3.35 that one's own duty, even imperfect, is better than another's.

key_terms.sense: acts in keeping with his own nature
even one who knows
beings follow their nature
what will forcible restraint achieve?

core_teaching: Everyone, even the wise, acts out of their ingrained nature, so sheer suppression achieves little; the work is to understand that nature and not be ruled by its likes and dislikes (3.34).

commentaries.gist: Nature is the store of past impressions showing at birth; even the knower acts by it, the ignorant all the more, so prohibition seems powerless. He raises the objection that effort and teaching are then pointless, answered in 3.34.

Even a wise person who knows from scripture that the self differs from matter is carried along by habits formed in past association with matter; against such ingrained tendencies, what can scripture's restraint do?

Answers why everyone doesn't simply do their duty unattached: disposition, shaped by past impressions, is powerful; even a wise man aware of good and bad acts according to it, so what can mere restraint of the senses do?
Warns that this verse does not mean there is no room for effort: read it with 3.34, which shows one can master nature by rising above liking and disliking; the steady meditator controls it.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to self-change: forcing yourself against your grain rarely lasts; know your temperament, work with it, and watch your likes and dislikes rather than fighting yourself head-on.
misreadings: Not 'I can't change, it's my nature'. The next verse says not to come under the sway of likes and dislikes.
Not a dismissal of discipline; it questions brute suppression.
cautions: Read alone, it can sound fatalistic; always pair with 3.34.
speaks_to: Repeated failure with willpower-only resolutions
Accepting one's temperament in career and relationships
Frustration that knowing better doesn't change behaviour
not_for: Someone excusing harmful behaviour as 'just my nature'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.34 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara (this is the scope of human effort).
context: Answers the fatalism that 3.33 might suggest. 3.35 follows with the teaching that one's own duty, even done imperfectly, is better than another's done well; then Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will (3.36).

key_terms.sense: in the object of each and every sense
attraction and aversion lie set, waiting
one should not come under their control
highwaymen, enemies on the road

core_teaching: Every sense meets its objects with built-in liking and disliking; you cannot stop these arising, but you can refuse to be ruled by them, and that is where effort counts.

commentaries.gist: Here lies the scope for effort: nature drags a person only through liking and aversion, toward neglecting one's own duty. Whoever checks these with their opposite follows the teaching, not his nature; they are enemies, like robbers on the road.

Every sense object attracts love from old habit and aversion when enjoyment is blocked; these grip whoever attempts the path of knowledge and drive him back to his inherited nature, so they are his strongest enemies.

If inclination follows nature, are injunctions useless? No: liking for pleasant objects and aversion to unpleasant ones are fixed in every sense, yet scripture says not to come under their sway, for they block the way.

Here lies the scope for personal effort: nature pulls through the two currents of attraction and aversion; control them by discrimination and inquiry and you can conquer nature and attain lasting peace.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a pause practice: notice the pull or the push before acting, name it, and choose instead of reacting; you don't have to obey every craving or irritation.
misreadings: Not 'never like or dislike anything'; it is about not being ruled.
Not self-hatred toward one's desires.
speaks_to: Reactivity, irritation, impulsive choices
Cravings around food, phone, spending
Decisions clouded by personal preference
not_for: Someone already rigidly over-controlled or scrupulous

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.38 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Our translation supplies 'wisdom' for idam ('this'), following Shankara and Sridhara, who answer from 3.39 that it is knowledge. Govindacharya's Ramanuja takes 'this' as all creatures, the world, wrapped in desire; Sivananda gives both. Acceptable, but note it is interpretive. Our_note's claim that later commentators (Madhusudana) read the three images as three depths of covering could not be checked in the sources used here; Sridhara says only that desire covers knowledge 'in all three ways'.
context: Arjuna has asked what drives a person to do wrong even against his will (3.36). Krishna answers that it is desire, which turns into anger, the all-consuming enemy (3.37). This verse illustrates how desire covers; 3.39 names what is covered, knowledge, and 3.40 says where desire lives: senses, mind and intellect.

key_terms.sense: fire is covered by smoke
a mirror by dust
an embryo by the womb's membrane
so this is covered by that (desire)

core_teaching: Desire veils clear seeing as smoke veils fire, dust a mirror and the membrane an unborn child: the light is still there, but hidden, to different degrees.

commentaries.gist: As a bright fire is wrapped in the dark smoke born with it, so 'this' is covered by desire; he then asks what 'this' is and answers with the next verse: knowledge.
'This' is the whole world of creatures, immersed in desire as fire is wrapped in smoke, a mirror's brightness dimmed by a stain, or an embryo sheathed in its membrane.
Shows desire's hostile nature: as fire is covered by its own smoke, a mirror by outside dust, and a foetus fully sealed by its membrane, so knowledge is covered by desire in all three ways.
'This' means the universe and also knowledge; 'that' which covers it is desire.

practical_reading: Teachers use the images to encourage: clarity is not lost, only covered; sometimes a little effort clears it (dust), sometimes it takes patience and time (the womb).
misreadings: Not 'all desire is evil'; the subject is the desire that drives one to wrongdoing (3.36-37).
Not a statement about pregnancy or embryos as impure; it is an image of covering.
cautions: The womb image could feel odd or sensitive for readers dealing with pregnancy or pregnancy loss.
speaks_to: Feeling that craving or obsession has clouded judgment
Wanting hope that clarity can return
Understanding why we act against our better judgment
not_for: Readers in pregnancy loss, if the embryo image is foregrounded
research_note: Earlier draft cited Madhusudana from a source we no longer use; that claim is now unverified.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.39 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara. Shankara explains anala as never having enough, no limit to its consuming; Sridhara reads it as 'like fire', since it is never satisfied and leads to grief.
context: Explains 3.38: what desire covers is knowledge. 3.40 names desire's seats (senses, mind, intellect), and 3.41 begins the remedy: first control the senses.

key_terms.sense: knowledge is covered
by the constant enemy of the wise
in the form of desire
hard to fill, a fire that never says 'enough'

core_teaching: Desire is like a fire that can never be filled; it covers even a wise person's understanding, and the wise feel it as an enemy all along, not only after the damage is done.

commentaries.gist: The wise know even beforehand that desire leads them astray, so it is their constant enemy; the ignorant treat it as a friend while craving and learn otherwise only when suffering comes. It never has enough.

The wise person's understanding of the self is clouded by an eternal foe disguised as lust, which breeds fascination with enjoyment; it is insatiable and inexhaustible, wanting another thing as soon as it gets one.

To the ignorant, desire brings pleasure during enjoyment and harm after; to the wise, who remember its harm, it is pain even then, hence their constant enemy. Never satisfied however fed, and leading to grief, it is like fire.

Quotes Manu: desire grows with enjoyment as fire with ghee; all the wealth of the earth would not satisfy one man of desire. The ignorant welcome desire as a friend; the wise know beforehand it brings misery.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the treadmill of wanting: getting what you crave rarely ends the craving, it feeds it; noticing this early is the first freedom.
misreadings: Not condemnation of all wishes and aspirations; it concerns compulsive craving.
Not shaming people for desires; it names a universal pattern.
speaks_to: Consumerism, endless scrolling, chasing the next upgrade
Addictive patterns
Ambition that never feels satisfied
not_for: Someone in early recovery who may hear 'enemy' as self-condemnation, unless framed gently

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.41 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. Prajahi can mean 'slay' or 'cast off'; Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara has 'cast off', Sridhara gives both 'destroy' and 'give up'. Our 'cast off' is fine. Our_note matches Shankara's gloss of jñāna (knowledge from scripture and teacher) and vijñāna (personal experience of it).
context: Krishna has named desire as the enemy that covers knowledge (3.37-39) and said it lodges in the senses, mind and intellect (3.40). This verse begins the remedy: start with the senses. 3.42-43 then point to what is higher than the senses, mind and intellect, and close the chapter with the call to slay desire.

key_terms.sense: first bringing the senses under control
the sinful one, the wrongdoer (desire)
slay, or cast off
destroyer of knowledge and of its direct realisation

core_teaching: Because desire works through the senses, begin there: get the senses in hand first, then cast off the desire that wrecks both learning and lived understanding.

commentaries.gist: First master the senses, then cast off desire, the sinful destroyer of jñāna, knowledge of the self learned from scripture and teacher, and vijñāna, the personal experience of what was taught. Next he asks where one stands to do this.

Desire breeds dislike for the self and love for sense pleasures; so steer the senses from their natural pursuits into the duties of karma yoga, and vanquish this great sinner that destroys knowledge and deeper knowledge of the self.

Control senses, mind and intellect at the very outset, before delusion sets in, and kill or give up sinful desire, which destroys both self-knowledge and scriptural knowledge (or knowledge from teaching and knowledge from meditation).
Jñāna is indirect knowledge from scripture; vijñāna is direct experience through self-realisation. Control the senses first, then kill desire.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as 'start with the doorway': manage what you see, hear and consume (screens, environments, company) before trying to wrestle with the craving itself.
misreadings: Not hatred of the body or the senses; it is about where to begin.
Not that every desire is sinful; the 'sinful one' is the compulsive desire of 3.37.
cautions: Violent language ('slay') and 'sinful' may feed self-hatred in a struggling reader; frame as steady practice.
speaks_to: Breaking a habit by changing environment and inputs
Students struggling with focus
Anyone whose cravings keep undoing what they know
not_for: Someone with harsh self-criticism or scrupulosity

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.42 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Two cautions. (1) 'Higher than the body' is not in the Sanskrit; it is Shankara's gloss (the senses are superior compared with the gross body); Sridhara instead says superior to their objects. Mark it as implied or drop it. (2) 'Self' for saḥ ('he/that') follows Shankara and Sridhara; Govindacharya's Ramanuja reads saḥ as desire itself, which overpowers even the intellect, and says reading it as the self is a mistake. Our reading is the majority one but not the only one.
context: After telling Arjuna to begin by controlling the senses (3.41), Krishna lays out a ladder of inner faculties, senses, mind, intellect and what lies beyond. 3.43 concludes: knowing what is beyond the intellect, steady yourself and slay desire. Chapter 4 then turns to the ancient lineage of this teaching.

key_terms.sense: the senses, they say, are high (subtle, inner)
the mind that forms and weighs intentions
the intellect that decides
and what is beyond the intellect is he (the self; Ramanuja: desire)

core_teaching: There is an order within: senses, then mind, then intellect, and beyond the intellect the self, the witness of all; knowing this ladder shows where to stand when fighting desire.

commentaries.gist: Compared with the gross body the senses are subtler and wider; mind, made of wishes and doubts, is above them; intellect, which decides, is above mind; above intellect is the self, its witness, whom desire bewilders by veiling knowledge.

Reads the series as obstacles to self-knowledge: senses, then the mind, then the misdirected intellect; and 'that' beyond the intellect is desire, rooted in the heart, which asserts mastery even when everything else is quiet.

Shows the self, on which the mind can be fixed to control the senses: senses are subtler than objects, mind directs senses, intellect decides before mind wills, and beyond the intellect, its innermost witness, is the self.

Senses are subtler than the body; the mind directs the senses; the intellect, able to discriminate, rescues the doubting mind; the self, the witness, is above the intellect, which borrows its light from the self.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a map of inner authority: the senses pull, the mind deliberates, the intellect decides, and your deepest self watches all of them; act from the top of the ladder, not the bottom.
misreadings: Not a ranking of people by intelligence.
Not a denial of the body's worth.
speaks_to: Feeling ruled by impulses
Wanting a simple model of the inner life
Meditation and self-observation
not_for: A reader in acute emotional distress who needs comfort rather than a model
research_note: Katha Upanishad cross-reference (the similar ladder of senses, mind, intellect, self) is from general knowledge of the text, not from a page read for this entry.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.43 (same numbering in all editions checked; last verse of chapter 3).
translation_note: Good, following Shankara and Sridhara. Govindacharya's Ramanuja reads 'that which is beyond the intellect' as desire and 'steadying the self by the self' as steadying the mind with the intellect, firmly resolving to fix it on the self.
context: The closing verse of chapter 3, completing the answer to Arjuna's question about what drives people to wrongdoing (3.36). Chapter 4 opens with Krishna revealing the ancient lineage of this teaching (4.1).

key_terms.sense: knowing what is beyond the intellect
steadying the self (mind) by the self
slay the enemy that has the form of desire
hard to get at, hard to overcome

core_teaching: Knowing the self that stands beyond even the intellect, and steadying the mind from that place, one can overcome desire, the enemy that is so hard to pin down.

commentaries.gist: Knowing the self as higher than the intellect, and composing the mind by the purified mind, slay desire, which is hard to conquer because its nature is complex and hard to grasp.

Know that desire, which can overpower even the intellect, is the enemy of the path of knowledge; firmly resolve to keep the mind established in the self, and destroy this inveterate foe in the shape of lust.
Desire and the like are changes in the intellect, while the self is their changeless witness; knowing this, pacify the mind by the intellect so convinced, and kill this hard-to-subdue enemy.

Restrain the lower self by the higher. Desire is hard to conquer but not impossible: discrimination, dispassion and steady practice overcome it, raising sattva overpowers rajas, and the direct way is prayer and repeating God's name.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to standing in your deepest self when cravings arise: from that place, watch the mind and steady it rather than being swept along; the struggle is real but winnable.
misreadings: Not violence toward oneself; 'slay' is aimed at compulsive desire.
Not 'desire is easy to beat'; the verse calls it hard to overcome.
cautions: Martial language ('slay the enemy') can feed self-hatred; frame as steadying, not attacking oneself.
speaks_to: Long struggles with a habit or craving
Wanting to act from one's best self
Building inner steadiness
not_for: Someone in a crisis of self-blame

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.7 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara. Note that both Shankara and Ramanuja define the dharma that declines in terms of the Vedic order of varṇa and āśrama; a modern reading should not import caste.
context: Krishna has told Arjuna that he first taught this yoga to Vivasvan (4.1); Arjuna asks how, since Vivasvan lived long before (4.4). Krishna answers that both have had many births, which he remembers (4.5), and that, though unborn, he takes birth through his own power (4.6). This verse and 4.8 say when and why he comes.

key_terms.sense: decline, weakening of dharma
the rise of adharma
I bring myself forth, manifest myself

core_teaching: Whenever the order that sustains life weakens and its opposite rises, the divine comes into the world: there is no fixed schedule, only the need.

commentaries.gist: Dharma here is the religion embodied in the order of castes and stages of life, the means to prosperity and liberation; whenever it decays and its opposite rises, the Lord manifests himself through his own maya.
No fixed periods are set for the Lord's incarnations: whenever and wherever the dharma of the varnas and ashramas declines and adharma grows, he manifests himself of his own free will.
Answers the question 'when do you come into being?': whenever righteousness decreases and unrighteousness predominates.
Dharma is what sustains and holds together, with no exact English equivalent: what elevates a person toward knowledge and liberation; adharma is what drags one down into worldliness and ignorance.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as hope in dark times: decline is not the end of the story. Many also read it as a call to take part in restoring what is right, rather than waiting passively.
misreadings: Not 'wait for rescue'. Many read it as a call to be the force that restores what is right.
Not a basis for declaring a particular leader or person an avatar.
cautions: Classical commentaries define dharma in caste terms (varṇa-āśrama); avoid carrying that into modern readings.
Political or communal misuse is common; keep it personal and ethical.
speaks_to: Despair at injustice or decline in society, workplace or family
Feeling that goodness is losing
Hope during dark periods
not_for: Someone waiting passively for a rescuer in an unsafe situation
Communal or political contexts where it could be used against others

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.8 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara.
context: Completes 4.7: why the Lord comes. 4.9 adds that whoever truly knows his divine birth and deeds is not born again but comes to him; 4.10 says many have reached his state this way.

key_terms.sense: to protect the good
and to destroy wrongdoers
to establish dharma firmly
age after age

core_teaching: The divine comes into the world, again and again, to protect the good, end the harm done by wrongdoers and set dharma back on its feet.

commentaries.gist: The good are those on the right path. Comments briefly; with 4.9 he adds that the Lord's birth is through maya, divine and not ordinary, and one who knows it truly is liberated.
The good are devotees who cannot live without seeing him, for whom a moment apart is an age; he comes so they may see him, to destroy evildoers, and to restore Vedic dharma, the mode of his worship.
He comes to protect those doing their duties, slay those who do vile deeds, and so make dharma secure. Chastising the wicked is not cruelty, any more than a mother disciplining her child.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society) (commentary printed under 4.7-8)
commentaries.gist: The good are those who live righteously, serve others with their bodies, and are free of selfishness, lust and greed; the Lord comes in every age to protect them and restore righteousness.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as reassurance that goodness is protected, and as an invitation to align with that protecting work through one's own fairness and courage.
misreadings: Not a licence to punish people you judge wicked; the work of setting right belongs to the divine and to justice.
Not 'my side is the good side'.
cautions: 'Destroy the wicked' can be weaponised in conflict; avoid in contexts of anger at a specific person.
May raise the question 'why wasn't I protected?' for someone who has suffered harm.
speaks_to: Feeling unprotected or overwhelmed by wrongdoing around you
Hope for justice
Ramanuja's reading: longing for God's presence
not_for: Someone wanting revenge
A victim of harm who may hear it as a broken promise

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.10 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara. 'Found their way home' in the line is a poetic gloss for 'attained my state' (mad-bhāvam), acceptable.
context: Follows 4.9: whoever truly knows Krishna's divine birth and deeds is not reborn but comes to him. Here he says many have reached that state. 4.11 adds that he meets each person in the way they approach him.

key_terms.sense: free of craving, fear and anger
absorbed in me, full of me
taking refuge in me
purified by the austerity that is knowledge
have come to my state, my being

core_teaching: Many before you have let go of craving, fear and anger, given themselves wholly to the Lord, been purified by understanding and reached his own state: the path is well travelled.

commentaries.gist: 'Absorbed in me' means knowing Brahman, seeing their identity with the Lord; 'refuge in me' means firm devotion to knowledge alone. Knowledge is itself the austerity, needing no other; purified by its fire, many have reached liberation.
Countless souls, free of desire, fear and anger, wholly given to and relying on him, have been purified by meditating on the truth of his incarnations and acts, and have come to his state.

Knowing his compassion in protecting dharma through his incarnations, people grow free of attachment, fear and anger, fix their minds on him, and purified by self-knowledge and duty done as austerity, both by his grace, attain his being.

Self-knowledge ends attachment; knowing oneself as the deathless self ends fear; seeing the self everywhere leaves no room for anger. The fire of wisdom burns latent tendencies, cravings and sins as fire burns cotton.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as encouragement: craving, fear and anger can be outgrown, and many ordinary people have done it through devotion and understanding; you are not the first.
misreadings: Not 'never feel fear or anger'; it describes where the path leads.
speaks_to: Anxiety or anger one wants to outgrow
Feeling alone on a spiritual path
Fear and attachment that keep one from trusting
not_for: Someone whose anger is a healthy response to injustice they need to address
A reader in acute anxiety who may feel judged for still being afraid

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.11 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Translation good. The line 'Every path, in its own way, leads to me' goes further than the Sanskrit and the commentaries. The verse says people follow Krishna's path in every way (sarvaśaḥ). Sridhara does say worshippers of Indra and other gods are really walking his path; but Shankara says he gives each what they seek (results to result-seekers, knowledge to the dutiful, liberation to seekers of liberation, relief to the distressed), and Ramanuja reads it as Krishna taking whatever form his devotees choose to approach him in. Suggest: 'However people come to me, I meet them there. In every way, people are walking my path.'
context: After saying that many have reached his state (4.10), Krishna answers an implied charge of favouritism. In 4.12 he notes that people who want quick results from action worship the gods, since success from action comes quickly in the human world.

key_terms.sense: in whatever way people approach me
in that same way I receive, favour them
they follow my path
in every way, on every side

core_teaching: The Lord responds to each person according to how they approach him, without favouritism; in all their ways of seeking, people are in some sense following his path.

commentaries.gist: He rewards each as they seek him: desired ends to seekers of fruit, knowledge to the dutiful, liberation to renouncers, relief to the distressed; never from favour or aversion. All follow the path of the Lord in all forms.

Not only through incarnations: in whatever form or way his devotees choose to conceive and seek him, he adapts himself and appears to them, so that they can enjoy him with every faculty, though he transcends thought and speech.

Is he partial, uniting only his devotees to himself? No: whether people worship with desires or without, he blesses them with what they seek; even those worshipping Indra and other gods walk his path.
He grants each the objects sought according to their motives: what selfish worshippers ask for, liberation to those who seek self-knowledge unselfishly. He is partial to no one.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say God meets people where they are: in a crisis, in curiosity, in longing for results, or in pure love, the response comes in the form the seeker can receive.
misreadings: Not 'all paths are identical' or 'whatever you do leads to the same goal'; the classical readings are more nuanced.
Not 'God gives whatever you ask for'.
cautions: Interfaith readings should not claim the classical commentators taught that all religions lead to the same end.
speaks_to: Feeling one's way of praying or seeking is 'not right enough'
Interfaith families or friendships
Returning to faith after a gap
not_for: Someone who reads it as transactional ('I worshipped, why didn't I get what I asked?')
research_note: Earlier draft cited Madhva from a source we no longer use; dropped.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.18 (same numbering in Shankara/Mahadeva Sastri, Ramanuja/Govindacharya, Sridhara/Vireswarananda and Sivananda).
attribution_note: Speaker and listener right. Our `setting` ('reveals the ancient lineage... why he comes into the world') describes 4.1-11; this verse belongs to 4.16-23, where Krishna says the nature of action is hard to grasp. Suggest: 'Krishna tells Arjuna that even the wise are confused about what action and inaction really are.'
translation_note: Translation good. Our_note follows Shankara and Sivananda (action belongs to body and senses, wrongly placed on the self; idleness is also action). Ramanuja reads it differently: seeing knowledge of the self (a-karma) within the work one does, and seeing contemplation itself as a kind of act; Sridhara: work offered to the Lord is no binding action, while skipping duty is action that binds. The line ('stillness inside activity') is a fair modern gloss of the Shankara/Sivananda reading.
context: Krishna has just said (4.16-17) that even sages are confused about what action is, and that action, wrong action and inaction must each be understood, for the way of action is deep. This verse states the paradox; 4.19-23 then describe the person whose actions are burnt up by knowledge, who acts without attachment and so is not bound.

key_terms.sense: inaction (non-binding, non-doing) seen within action
action seen within inaction (idleness is still doing)
truly wise, discerning
disciplined, integrated, a yogi
one who has done all that is to be done / performs all actions

core_teaching: Whether we are bound depends less on whether the body moves than on the doer behind it: work done without the sense 'I am the doer' or without craving for its fruit does not bind, while sitting idle with the ego intact is still action.

commentaries.gist: To the ignorant, true inaction looks like action and vice versa; both assume an agent, which belongs to ignorance. The self is actionless; one who sees this amid activity, and sees idleness as action, is wise.

A-karma here is knowledge of the self. The wise see that knowledge in the work they do, contemplating the self while working, and see contemplation itself as a kind of act; such a person is fit for liberation.
Work done as worship of the Lord is really inaction, since it leads to knowledge and does not bind; not doing prescribed duty is really action, leading to sin and bondage. One who sees this is wise.
Bondage comes from the idea 'I am the doer'. If one stands as witness of nature's activity, much work is no action; if one sits idle but keeps the idea of agency, that idleness is action.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to burnout and to procrastination alike: you can be extremely busy and inwardly quiet if you drop the anxious 'it all depends on me', and you can be lying on the sofa while your mind churns, which is still exhausting activity.
misreadings: Not permission to do nothing because 'everything is really inaction'.
Not a claim that what you do doesn't matter morally; Sridhara reads neglect of duty as binding action.
Not a productivity slogan about 'staying calm while busy' only; it is about the sense of doership.
cautions: Abstract and paradoxical; a reader in acute distress may find it confusing rather than steadying unless the reading explains it simply.
speaks_to: Burnout from feeling everything depends on oneself
Guilt about resting, or restlessness while resting
People caught between 'doing more' and 'stepping back'
Overthinkers whose minds stay busy when the body stops
not_for: Someone in depression being told their inactivity is 'really action' in a blaming way
A reader looking for concrete, practical instruction for a crisis today

context: Part of Krishna's portrait (4.19-23) of the one whose actions are 'burnt in the fire of knowledge'. 4.19 described one whose undertakings are free of desire-driven plans; this verse says such a person, though fully busy, does nothing; 4.21-22 add that he works with mind controlled, content with what comes, and is not bound.

ever content, satisfied (Ramanuja: content in the eternal self)
depending on nothing, needing no support for personal ends
he does not do anything at all (his action does not bind)

core_teaching: When attachment to results is gone and contentment comes from within, even full engagement in work does not create bondage; the action is, in effect, no action.

commentaries.gist: Having dropped concern for action and fruit through knowledge, content and seeking nothing for himself, he might give up action, but where that is impracticable works on as an example; knowing the actionless self, he does nothing.
Free of any link with results, content in the eternal self and not dependent on matter, such a person may seem intent on work, yet does nothing binding, since inwardly he is cultivating knowledge.

Giving up attachment to action and its fruit, content with his own bliss and so needing nothing for gaining or keeping, he does nothing even while fully engaged in natural or prescribed action; his actions become non-actions.

Repeats the idea of inaction in action for emphasis: one who works without egoism or attachment, for the world's good, does nothing though always active; like someone favoured by the king, he needs no lesser support.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to working hard without needing the outcome or others' validation to feel whole: give full effort, then let the result go, and the job stops eating you.
misreadings: Not 'do whatever you like, it doesn't count'.
Not indifference to the people affected by your work.
Not a call to stop caring about doing the work well.
cautions: 'Ever content' can sound like a standard a struggling reader fails; present it as a direction, not a test.
speaks_to: Overwork driven by the need to prove oneself
People whose mood rises and falls with each result at work
Caregivers and volunteers who give a lot and want to stop keeping score
Anyone dependent on praise or approval to feel settled
not_for: Someone being exploited at work, who might read it as 'don't care about pay or recognition'
A reader in grief or crisis who cannot yet feel 'content'
