context: Continues Krishna's portrait (4.19-23) of one who acts without binding. After 4.20 (content, dependent on nothing), this verse adds giving up expectation and possessiveness; 4.22 adds contentment with what comes unbidden and evenness in success and failure; 4.23 says the whole action of such a person melts away.

key_terms.sense: free of longing or expectation (not 'hopeless')
with mind and body (or self) restrained
having given up all possessions / possessiveness
mere bodily action: what the body needs (Shankara), or action done as a bodily function (Ramanuja)
fault, sin, taint

core_teaching: Action does not taint one who has dropped craving for outcomes and possessiveness and keeps mind and body in hand; Shankara applies it to the renunciate's bare upkeep, Ramanuja to any selfless worker.

commentaries.gist: One free of desire, mind and body controlled, owning nothing, doing only what bare bodily existence needs, incurs no sin; for a seeker of liberation even merit binds. 'Bodily action' cannot mean any act done with the body.

Without longing for fruit, with the mind's anxieties restrained, and giving up selfish love of material things, one who works for life as a mere bodily function incurs no evil, meaning samsara; such karma yoga alone leads to self-vision.

Free of desire, body and mind subdued, possessions relinquished, acting with the body but without sense of agency, he is not bound; for one with knowledge, natural acts like begging alms to sustain the body bring no sin.

The liberated sage keeps only actions needed for the body's maintenance and has given up possessions; for a seeker of liberation even righteousness is a golden fetter, and the sage is free of both good and evil.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that much of what wears us out is not the work but the grasping around it: expectations about outcomes and the urge to own and control. Doing simple, needed tasks without that grasping keeps the heart clean.
misreadings: Not 'live without hope' or 'expect nothing good from life'.
Not a demand to give away everything one owns (that is Shankara's reading for monks, not a rule for householders).
Not a license for any bodily act: Shankara explicitly rejects reading it as 'whatever is done with the body is sinless'.
cautions: Our current English 'without hope' could be read by a depressed user as endorsing hopelessness; fix before use.
Ideal of owning nothing can feel shaming to people anxious about money.
speaks_to: People exhausted by possessiveness and control
Those learning to do ordinary chores and work without resentment
Minimalists or people simplifying their lives
Anyone anxious about outcomes of daily work
not_for: Readers in despair or depression (unless the translation is fixed)
People facing financial hardship, for whom 'give up all possessions' lands badly

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.24 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good. Our translation renders arpaṇam as 'the act of offering'; Shankara and Ramanuja take it as the instrument of offering (ladle etc.), Sivananda as the oblation. Minor. Our_note's 'traditionally recited before meals' is widely known practice but was not stated in the sources read for this entry.
context: Krishna has just said (4.23) that the entire action of one who works as a sacrifice melts away. This verse gives the vision behind that: every element of the offering is Brahman. It opens a list (4.25-33) of the many kinds of sacrifice people perform, ending with the claim that the sacrifice of knowledge is highest.

key_terms.sense: the instrument or act of offering is Brahman
the oblation is Brahman
offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman
by one absorbed in Brahman in (all) action

core_teaching: For one who sees the one reality in every part of an act (the doer, the means, the offering, the receiver, the result), the act stops binding and becomes a path to that reality itself.

commentaries.gist: For one who knows Brahman, the ladle, oblation, fire, offerer, act and result are nothing but Brahman, as mistaken silver is only mother-of-pearl; so his action is no action. The verse praises knowledge by describing it as a sacrifice.

The ladle, oblation, fire and offerer are all effects of Brahman and so are Brahman; whoever contemplates every act as ensouled by Brahman reaches the self's Brahman-like nature, and work itself becomes knowledge and the means to self-vision.
This is the sacrifice of wisdom: the ideas of instrument, action and result are replaced by Brahman, so action melts away, as 4.23 says; for the self-realised, all life becomes such a sacrifice.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to ordinary tasks, especially eating and cooking: treat the food, the hands, the fire and the meal as sacred, and a routine act becomes worship. Many families say it as a grace before meals.
misreadings: Not literal ritual instruction about fire sacrifices.
Not pantheism in a casual 'everything is God, so nothing matters' sense; the commentators link it to knowledge or contemplation that changes how one acts.
cautions: Abstract metaphysics; pair with a concrete practice (e.g. a mindful meal) for readers who are struggling.
speaks_to: Bringing a sense of the sacred into routine chores and meals
People who feel their daily work is meaningless
Those wanting a short daily recitation
not_for: Someone with an eating disorder, if the reading centres on food
A reader wanting practical, problem-solving help today

context: Krishna has been extolling knowledge: it is the highest sacrifice (4.33), learned by approaching the wise with humility and service (4.34), and it carries even the worst wrongdoer across sin, burning actions as fire burns wood (4.36-37). This verse calls it the supreme purifier; 4.39-40 then name the qualities that win it and the doubt that loses it.

key_terms.sense: a purifier equal to knowledge
one made fit or perfected by yoga (karma yoga, and for Shankara also meditation)
in time, in due course
finds it within oneself

core_teaching: Understanding the self cleanses more deeply than any rite or penance, and it is not handed over from outside: it ripens within a person who has been made ready by steady practice, in its own time.

commentaries.gist: No purifier equals wisdom. The seeker of liberation who has made himself fit through karma yoga and the yoga of concentration will, after long practice, find that wisdom himself, within himself.

Nothing in the universe is as purifying as knowledge of the self; it destroys all sin. Perfected by practising karma yoga as taught, which is easy, one realises the self's nature within oneself in due course.
Among penances and yogas nothing purifies like knowledge. Why doesn't everyone pursue knowledge alone? Because it comes of itself, in time, only to one made fit by intense karma yoga, not without it.
There is no purifier like self-knowledge; one who has reached perfection through steady practice of karma yoga and meditation finds it in himself after a time.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage patience with inner growth: keep doing the practice and the work honestly, and clarity arrives on its own schedule, from within, rather than by forcing it.
misreadings: Not 'knowledge' as information or intellectual learning; it means insight into the self.
Not a promise of quick results ('in time' means after long practice, per Shankara).
cautions: 'Purifier' language can imply the reader is impure or guilty; frame it as clearing confusion rather than washing away sin for a reader carrying shame.
speaks_to: People feeling stuck in spiritual or personal practice
Those carrying guilt who want a path forward
Learners impatient for understanding
not_for: Someone in acute crisis needing immediate relief, for whom 'in due time' may feel dismissive

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.39 (same numbering in all editions checked).
translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara. Shankara and Sridhara read tat-paraḥ as devoted to the means of knowledge, especially serving and listening to the teacher (link to 4.34); the line's 'commitment' captures this.
context: Following 4.38 (knowledge as the supreme purifier, found within in time), Krishna names the three conditions for gaining it: faith, devotion to it, and mastery of the senses. 4.40 then describes the opposite case, the person of doubt, and 4.41-42 close the chapter by urging Arjuna to cut doubt with the sword of knowledge and rise.

key_terms.sense: one who has faith/trust (in the teaching and teacher)
devoted to it, intent on the means to knowledge
with senses restrained
supreme peace, before long

core_teaching: Trust, steady devotion to the means and self-restraint together bring real understanding, and understanding quickly brings deep peace.

commentaries.gist: Faith alone may be slow, so devotion to the means, like attending the teacher, is added; then sense-mastery. Together they surely bring wisdom, being impossible to fake, unlike outward show, and wisdom swiftly brings liberation.

Having received knowledge by instruction (4.34), growing ever more devoted as it ripens and drawing away from outward pulls of the senses, one soon reaches the height of wisdom and then supreme peace, spiritual bliss.

Only one who trusts the teacher's teaching, is wholly devoted to it and controls the senses gains knowledge; until then one follows the way of action to purify; after knowledge nothing remains to do and peace follows at once.

One who has faith, serves his teacher and hears his teaching, and has subdued the senses, surely gains knowledge and quickly reaches peace; all three qualifications are needed, one alone will not suffice.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to any real learning or healing: trust the process, keep showing up, and rein in distractions, and understanding comes, bringing a calm that outlasts moods.
misreadings: Not 'just believe and everything will be fine'; faith is one of three conditions.
Not blind obedience to any guru; the context is sincere study with a genuine teacher.
cautions: Faith framed as a condition can make a doubting reader feel excluded; pair with the reassurance that sincere effort counts.
speaks_to: People starting a practice or course of study
Those who have lost peace and want a path back
Readers rebuilding trust after confusion
not_for: Someone harmed by a manipulative teacher or religious authority
A reader in a faith crisis who may hear it as a reproach

translation_note: Good; our_note matches Shankara, who says the doubter is ruined most of all, 'the most sinful'. The misuse note ('questioning is welcome; this is corrosive doubt') is an editorial gloss, not from the commentaries, but fair: Ramanuja and Sridhara define the doubter as one who doubts the teaching already received (Sridhara: whether it will bear fruit in him). 'Perishes' (vinaśyati) is read by Sridhara as 'fails to reach his goal', not physical death.
context: After naming faith, devotion and self-control as the way to knowledge (4.39), Krishna describes the unfit seeker: ignorant, faithless or doubting. Next (4.41-42) he says actions do not bind one whose doubts are cut by knowledge, and urges Arjuna to cut the doubt in his heart with the sword of knowledge and stand up.

key_terms.sense: ignorant, uninstructed
without faith, not trusting the teaching
one whose mind is made of doubt
is ruined, fails to reach the goal

core_teaching: Of the obstacles to understanding, chronic doubt is the worst: it blocks not only spiritual progress but ordinary happiness, because nothing can be wholeheartedly begun or enjoyed.

commentaries.gist: The ignorant and the faithless are ruined, but not as much as the doubter, the most sinful of all: even this common world, the next, and happiness escape him, since he doubts them too. So do not doubt.

The ignorant lacks instruction, the non-earnest lacks fervour after instruction, the sceptic doubts what he received; one who doubts the self taught to him forfeits worldly goals and the next world, let alone liberation, since all depend on that conviction.

Describes the unfit seeker: one who hasn't grasped the teacher's teaching, or grasped it without faith, or has faith but doubts it will bear fruit in him. The doubter loses everything: wealth and marriage here, merit hereafter, and happiness.

The faithless lacks faith in himself, scripture and his teacher. The doubter's condition is deplorable: unsure of the next world, he cannot rejoice in this one either, being so suspicious; he has no happiness.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to paralysing second-guessing: constant doubt about every choice drains joy and stops all progress, so at some point you commit to a path and test it by living it.
misreadings: Not a ban on questions or critical thinking; Arjuna questions Krishna throughout.
Not a threat that doubters will be destroyed; 'perishes' means failing to reach the goal.
Not condemnation of someone wrestling honestly with faith.
cautions: Strong condemnatory language ('most sinful', 'perishes'); can wound readers with anxiety, OCD-type doubt, or faith struggles.
Should not be used with someone grieving who doubts God's goodness.
speaks_to: Chronic indecision and second-guessing
People who never commit to a path and feel stuck
Cynicism that has drained joy from life
not_for: Readers with anxiety or obsessive doubt, who may hear it as a verdict
Someone in a faith crisis after loss
Survivors of spiritual abuse who were punished for questioning

Ramanuja and Sridhara read yoga-saṃnyasta-karmāṇam as one who has dedicated or offered actions through karma yoga, not given them up; the translation's 'renounced action through yoga' allows both.

key_terms.sense: one who has renounced, or dedicated, actions through yoga
whose doubts are cut away by knowledge
self-possessed, vigilant, inwardly steady
actions do not bind

core_teaching: When action is offered or let go through yoga, doubt is cut by understanding, and the mind is steady and watchful, one's actions no longer chain one.

commentaries.gist: One who sees the Supreme renounces both merit and demerit through that knowledge, his doubt cut by realising the self's oneness with the Lord; seeing all action as the play of the gunas and ever watchful, he is not bound.

Works done by karma yoga from the standpoint of wisdom lose their binding power; doubts about the self are dispelled by self-knowledge; the mind reaches unshakable certainty; then no string of deeds can bind such a person.

Concludes chapters 3-4 on action then knowledge: one who offers actions to the Lord in worship, whose ego-sense about the body is destroyed by knowing he is not the agent, and who is alert, is not bound by actions.
Cites Madhusudana for 'ever watchful'. One established in the identity of individual and supreme soul has his doubts cut; his actions, burnt in the fire of wisdom, do not bind.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to acting with a clear head after a period of confusion: once you have thought it through and settled your doubt, act fully and steadily, offering the result, and stop being dragged back by every action's aftermath.
misreadings: Not 'nothing you do has consequences'.
Not suppressing doubts; the doubt is cut by understanding, not ignored.
cautions: Paired with 4.40's harsh view of doubt; keep the tone encouraging.
speaks_to: Moving from long indecision into committed action
People haunted by guilt over past actions
Those seeking inner steadiness at work
not_for: Someone avoiding responsibility for harm they've done, who might read it as 'my actions don't bind me'

the discipline of acting without attachment
both bring about the highest good
is distinguished, better

commentaries.gist: Renunciation and karma yoga both lead to liberation by giving rise to knowledge; but karma yoga is better than mere renunciation not accompanied by knowledge. Renunciation with knowledge, he notes, is a far higher path.

Renunciation here means ceasing from work, that is, the path of knowledge. Each path can independently lead to bliss, but karma yoga is better than the renunciation of works; the following verses explain why.

Both lead to liberation, but karma yoga is better than renunciation without self-knowledge, while renunciation with knowledge is superior; karma yoga is easy and so suits most people.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the urge to quit everything when overwhelmed: for most people the way through is not walking away but continuing to act while letting go of the grasping and resentment around the work.
misreadings: Not 'never rest, retire or take a break'.
Not a dismissal of monks or contemplative life; Shankara holds renunciation with knowledge to be higher.
Not 'activity for its own sake is good'.
cautions: Can sound like pressure to keep going for a burnt-out reader; pair with the point that the action meant is unattached, not driven.

Those torn between withdrawal and engagement
Retirees wondering how to stay meaningfully engaged

A person leaving an abusive situation, who should not read it as 'stay and keep acting'

context: Having said that karma yoga is better than renunciation (5.2), Krishna explains why: the person who neither hates nor craves is already a true renouncer, even while acting. In 5.4-5 he says only the immature see knowledge and action as different paths; both reach the same goal.

neither hates nor craves
free from the pairs of opposites
is easily freed from bondage

core_teaching: Renunciation is an inner state, not a robe or a place: whoever has stopped hating and craving is a renouncer while fully engaged in life, and is freed easily.

commentaries.gist: The karma yogi who neither hates pain and its causes nor desires pleasure and its sources is a perpetual renouncer, even while acting; free of the pairs, he is easily released. Sankhya and Yoga share one goal.

The karma yogi who has tasted the bliss of the self desires nothing but the self, so has nothing to hate and can endure the pairs; such a person is a constant renouncer, practising knowledge, and easily escapes bondage.

Praising the karma yogi as a renouncer shows why action is better: one free of attachment and aversion, working for the Lord, is a renouncer even while working, and being pure-minded is easily freed through knowledge.

Giving up work from laziness, family quarrels, calamity or unemployment does not make a renouncer; the karma yogi above liking and disliking, success and failure, praise and blame, is one, even without formal vows.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to people who think peace requires leaving: you don't need to move to a monastery or quit your life; dropping resentment and craving where you are is the real letting go.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all feeling; it concerns hatred and craving.
Not 'you are a renunciate, so you have no obligations'.
cautions: A reader full of anger or longing may feel judged; present it as a direction, not a test they are failing.
speaks_to: People who fantasise about escaping their lives to find peace
Householders who feel spiritually second-class
Those working on resentment or envy
not_for: Someone whose anger is a healthy response to injustice or abuse

key_terms.sense: with body, mind and intellect
with the senses alone, free of ego (Shankara) or without engrossment (Sridhara)
giving up attachment (to results)
for purification of the self or mind

Free of clinging to fruits such as heaven, karma yogis let body, mind, intellect and senses do the work as instruments of self-purification, which means breaking the bonds of past deeds on the self.

cautions: 'Purification' can imply the reader is dirty or guilty; frame as clarity.

having let go of the fruit of action
attains peace born of steadfastness, lasting peace
under the drive of desire
is bound fast

core_teaching: The same work can free or bind: done with the result handed over, it brings lasting peace; done in the grip of desire for the result, it chains the doer.

commentaries.gist: The steady one, resolved 'I act for the Lord, not for my benefit', gives up the fruit and reaches liberation by stages: purity of mind, knowledge, renunciation of action, steadiness in knowledge. The unsteady, led by desire, is firmly bound.

The right performer wants nothing but the self, gives up the fruit and works only to purify himself, reaching the lasting joy of the self; the one who craves other fruits, driven by lust, stays bound in samsara.

Answers how the same actions bind some and free others: the one devoted solely to the Lord, acting without seeking fruit, gains liberation; the outward-turned one, impelled by desire and attached to fruit, is completely bound.
The harmonious person says 'I act for my Lord, not for gain' and reaches peace through four stages; the unbalanced person thinking 'I did this and will get that' is firmly bound.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to work and relationships: do your part fully and let go of controlling the payoff; the more you need a particular outcome, the more every setback owns you.
misreadings: Not refusing fair pay, recognition or planning; it is about not being chained to them (as our misuse note says).
Not passivity about outcomes that affect others.
cautions: 'Bound' language can feel judgmental to someone anxious about money or results; keep the tone compassionate.
speaks_to: Anxiety about results at work or in exams
People whose self-worth hangs on outcomes
Founders, salespeople, students under pressure
Those recovering from disappointment after a big effort
not_for: Someone in financial crisis who might hear 'don't care about the money'
A reader in fresh grief over an outcome that cannot be undone
